To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the CCF of dense systems is a fingerprint of their local order and symmetry, and that at partial coherence, the CCOF of dense systems corresponds to that of the individual objects.

we have shown how to extract information on the sample symmetry from the cross-correlation of diffraction patterns, even in the presence of transverse beam coherence, and that this technique can provide an atomic-scale resolution in real space, with the potential to reach femtosecond time resolution.
the cross-correlation functions of diffraction patterns of two-dimensional dense mono- disperse systems are a fingerprint of the local order in the sample.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of the CCF as a tool to investigate the static and dynamic structure of colloidal systems, with the aim of developing a technique to study in real time the evolution of the local ordering of colloidal particles in the liquid phase.
the development and application of coherent diffraction imaging techniques to the study of the static and dynamical structure of complex materials.

the development of new techniques for the characterization of the structure and dynamics of materials, in particular for the investigation of the structural changes in dense colloidal systems, where the interplay between the particle’s size, shape and interactions is of primary importance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the cross-correlation is a powerful tool for the analysis of the local structure of a sample, provided that the sample is not too large with respect to the beam coherence, and the sample is sufficiently ordered.
the CCF is not a reliable tool for retrieving the structural information in dense samples.
the CCF of dense samples is a fingerprint of local order in the sample and is independent of beam coherence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, at partial transverse coherent illumination, the diffraction patterns from a dense system of scattering objects can be considered as a superposition of those from individual objects.
the CCF analysis is able to retrieve information about both static and dynamic properties of the sample, and that the CCF amplitude is directly proportional to the degree of order in the sample.
the CCF analysis of diffraction data from dense systems is a powerful tool to retrieve information about their local structure and symmetry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
in order to retrieve the structural information on dense systems, the CCF must be calculated at full transverse coherence of both the probe and the sample.
in the case of dense systems, the coherence of the beam is not a necessary condition for the CCF to retrieve structural properties.
the CCF analysis is a powerful tool in the study of dense systems.
